title: Partial and Complete Observables for Hamiltonian Constrained Systems
relevance: Prior art for clock-based relational/complete observables and gauge-invariant extensions; conceptual support only for the present marked-geodesic construction.
version: arXiv:gr-qc/0411013v1, submitted 2004-11-02; journal version Gen. Rel. Grav. 39 (2007), 1891–1927
locator: Sections 1, 3, 7, 10–11; arXiv HTML lines 39–52 for framing; the paper develops complete observables from clocks and partial observables, with infinitely many clock variables for field-theory embeddings
assumptions: Hamiltonian constrained/gauge systems; complete-observable constructions require clock/gauge-flow assumptions developed in the paper. This lane uses it as conceptual prior art, not as a proof of the geodesic covariance lemma or of a coupled-solution separation.
conclusion: Relational clock plus partial observable constructions are established prior work; background-independent field theories require embedding information, and complete observables have gauge structure.
proof_status: Full text inspected at stated sections; no independent reproduction of the paper's proofs.
dependencies: Canonical constrained-system framework and cited Rovelli/Kuchar work.
open_questions: No direct theorem located here establishing the exact marked-geodesic observable or full-past matched solutions required by the present target; no novelty inference.
limits: This is canonical constrained-system prior art, not a proof of the spacetime geodesic lemma. The field-theory discussion uses embedding clocks; exact hypotheses and the cited proofs were not independently audited. It supplies no full-past matching or coupled-solution separation result for this project.

title: Why do all the curvature invariants of a gravitational wave vanish?
relevance: Primary counterexample to treating curvature scalar invariants as complete tests of local gravitational curvature; motivates observer-marked tidal outcomes.
locator: Sections 2–3, especially the proposition at HTML lines 67–93 and plane-wave discussion at lines 96–104. States nonflat indefinite-signature examples for which curvature invariants of arbitrary finite derivative order vanish; gives the vacuum pp-wave form and condition.
assumptions: Smooth indefinite-signature metrics and the paper's continuous scalar curvature-invariant definition; plane wave/pp-wave metrics as specified in Sec. 3.
conclusion: Vanishing curvature scalars, including for the displayed plane waves, does not imply flatness; curvature scalars alone can miss nonzero curvature.
proof_status: Full text inspected for cited statements and argument; no independent rederivation of the proposition.
dependencies: Differential geometry of pseudo-Riemannian metrics; no computational dependency.
open_questions: Does not analyze observer-marked tidal measurements, matter matching, or lawful-completion constructions.
limits: The cited result concerns mathematical Lorentzian metrics and scalar curvature-invariant classes, not the existence of a common-matter-model completion pair. The paper's plane-wave example supports incompleteness of scalar tests; it does not establish any matched-observer measurement or detector response.

title: Nonvanishing Local Scalar Invariants even in VSI Spacetimes with all Polynomial Curvature Scalar Invariants Vanishing
relevance: Qualifies the curvature-scalar obstruction by showing that some nonpolynomial local invariants can detect generic plane-wave amplitudes, while carrying added definedness assumptions.
locator: Sections I–III and IX; HTML lines 47–54 define the VSI scope and motivate curvature-selected null-direction constructions; lines 94–124 calculate exact plane-wave curvature and a nonpolynomial scalar example, including its definedness conditions; lines 282–287 summarize scope.
assumptions: VSI means all scalar contractions of polynomials in Riemann and its covariant derivatives vanish; the paper constructs additional nonpolynomial local scalar quantities using curvature-selected null directions, subject to genericity/definedness conditions.
conclusion: Polynomial curvature scalar invariants can all vanish in nonflat wave geometries; alternative scalar constructions are possible under added structure and genericity assumptions.
proof_status: Inspected full text at the stated definitions, plane-wave calculations and conclusion; not an independent proof audit or reproduction of every construction.
open_questions: The paper's alternative invariants have domain/genericity restrictions and are not a substitute for specifying the observer apparatus or a detector model.
limits: The alternative invariants are nonpolynomial and depend on auxiliary null-direction optimization; their definedness/genericity restrictions matter. This paper does not give a detector model, a full-past matching construction, or a coupled-theory separation theorem.

title: Observables for General Relativity related to geometry
authors: Paweł Duch, Wojciech Kamiński, Jerzy Lewandowski, Jędrzej Świeżewski
relevance: Prior-art lead for observer-based GR observables; the abstract's stated spatial-diffeomorphism invariance is narrower than the spacetime covariance lemma here.
locator: Abstract: observer-based scheme for invariant observables, reported invariant under spatial diffeomorphisms preserving the observer; full text was not accessed in this pass.
assumptions: Canonical/observer-based construction as described in abstract; scope is spatial diffeomorphism invariance, which is weaker than the spacetime covariance claim proved directly here.
conclusion: Observer-marked relational observables in GR have established prior art, with a specifically stated residual spatial-diffeomorphism scope.
proof_status: Abstract only; no theorem/proof claims imported.
dependencies: Canonical GR and observer construction (not audited).
open_questions: Exact residual gauge hypotheses and relation to a spacetime geodesic observable require full-text audit; access gate for any stronger claim.
limits: Only the abstract was read, so the construction's detailed hypotheses, proof and residual gauge freedom remain unverified here. It is used solely as a prior-art lead for observer-based observables, not as evidence for the spacetime geodesic lemma or lawful-completion separation.
